chapter: Miles Davis stories and what jazz means
title: Police harassment of Gil and Anita in Los Angeles
summary: Gil describes police following the interracial couple and a ticket outside a club where Miles was playing.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Out in California they are like that a lot. That's one of the reasons why Anita and I don't like the idea of moving to Southern California, Hollywood because they are very peculiar out there.

Every time I looked in the rear vision mirror in the car that we rented when we were out there the police were following us on a motorcycle because we were an integrated couple. It's fantastic. Really fantastic.
And of course, it just simply doesn't occur to these people that she could possibly be your legitimate wife.

We were out in front of the club that Miles was playing, the E It Club out in Los Angeles and it was a regular kind, like a neighborhood club, you know. People kind of wanted to hear Miles Davis play, wasn't a chic place. So, I parked the car across the street. When I came out it was about 4 in the morning and there had been a dark red stripe along the curb that had been painted there. You couldn't even see it. But a cop gave me

a ticket.
Well that ended up with him wanting to search everybody and he's been saying to me, what do you do? And I said, well I'm a composer. And he said, well I hope you don't write jazz, something like that. Imagine a cop bothering to say that to me.

He's got Harold up against the car and Harold's turned around. It's really fantastic over nothing.
It was because we were all mixed together that was it. We were all mixed together. There were a couple of, Miles and I were writing a score for a play at the time that Lawrence Harvey was going to play in. Lawrence Harvey was there, (he was an actor, a famous actor?). It was a mixture like that and that policeman took it upon himself to be the cultural dictator besides the social director of the city. (LAUGHTER).
They really do that, they really do that.
